articles.title: Schema.org for Transport Services: How We Built a Rich Entity Graph That Google Actually Reads
articles.excerpt: Most transport booking sites slap a basic LocalBusiness schema on their homepage and call it done. We went deeper — building a connected entity graph that links our operator, services, vehicles, and r…
articles.body: Most transport booking sites slap a basic LocalBusiness schema on their homepage and call it done. We went deeper — building a connected entity graph that links our operator, services, vehicles, and routes across 633 pages in 8 languages. Here's what we learned. The Problem with Basic Schema A typical transport site might have this on their homepage: { "@type" : "LocalBusiness" , "name" : "Some Transfer Company" , "telephone" : "+1234567890" } This tells Google almost nothing useful. It doesn't describe what you do, where you operate, what vehicles you use, or how your services connect to the places you serve.

articles.title: AI Says This 20% Gap Can Never Be Closed. Can You Prove It Wrong?
articles.excerpt: Ten years ago I worked at a mobile game company. To speed up our gateway, I wrote enif_protobuf — Erlang has no official protobuf runtime, so I built a C core + NIF that raised gateway throughput seve…
articles.body: Ten years ago I worked at a mobile game company. To speed up our gateway, I wrote enif_protobuf — Erlang has no official protobuf runtime, so I built a C core + NIF that raised gateway throughput several times over pure Erlang code (today's Erlang table still shows ~3.9x encode / ~2.3x decode vs pure-Erlang gpb). Recently, with AI help, I ported that same dynamic design into pbwire : one C core, 23 language bindings, each benchmarked against its official counterpart. All numbers are in BENCHMARKS.md . One rule: stay dynamic. Load a standard FileDescriptorSet at runtime, no per-message generated code, and bytes must match protoc exactly before anything is timed. It won almost everywhere. Java (pure Java, no JNI) does 1.13x / 1.95x on the 74KB tier.

articles.title: Signal2Speech: answering questions with an EEG headset at Hack the Nest 2026
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the MLH x DEV Writing Challenge My team, Order of the Golden Eagles, built Signal2Speech, an accessibility prototype for people who have difficulty speaking or typing. People…
articles.body: This is a submission for the MLH x DEV Writing Challenge What I Built My team, Order of the Golden Eagles, built Signal2Speech, an accessibility prototype for people who have difficulty speaking or typing. People with conditions like ALS, stroke, or cerebral palsy can lose the ability to speak or type, even though they still know exactly what they want to say. Most assistive tools either make them spell out every letter, which is slow, or guess for them, which takes the decision out of their hands. Our main rule came from that: the app suggests what to say, but the wearer decides what they actually want to say. A conversation partner types a question, and Claude suggests two short replies based only on facts the app has verified.

articles.title: Stop Asking AI Coding Agents for Days: Build a Calibrated Time Estimator
articles.excerpt: Ask a coding agent how long a task will take and it may answer in human calendar units: “a few hours,” “one or two days,” or “about a week.” Then it finishes the code change in twelve minutes, or spen…
articles.body: Ask a coding agent how long a task will take and it may answer in human calendar units: “a few hours,” “one or two days,” or “about a week.” Then it finishes the code change in twelve minutes, or spends an afternoon chasing a broken test. The estimate sounds confident, but it may not be grounded in observed behavior from comparable tasks. A small project called AI Time Estimator, shared on Hacker News on November 15, takes a different route. It uses local Claude Code transcripts to estimate the agent’s working time, then compares estimates with completed sessions and adjusts future ranges. Its author describes a read-only estimator, local data, and a feedback loop.

articles.title: My Loss Went NaN, and a 2016 Textbook Explained Why
articles.excerpt: Every deep learning journey has the same plot twist: the loss curve goes flat, or worse, turns into NaN at epoch 3 like it just discovered nihilism. The framework error says nothing useful. Stack Over…
articles.body: Every deep learning journey has the same plot twist: the loss curve goes flat, or worse, turns into NaN at epoch 3 like it just discovered nihilism. The framework error says nothing useful. Stack Overflow says "lower your learning rate." You lower it by 10x. Nothing changes—now it just reaches NaN with more dignity. The first time this happened to me, I had written a custom classification loop where I manually applied torch.softmax() at the end of forward() and then fed the probabilities into torch.log() inside my own cross-entropy function. On clean toy inputs, it looked fine.

articles.body: 1. Pain – When DRAM procurement still runs on manual labor At 8 a.m. on Monday, Minh, the procurement director of an electronics factory in Bac Ninh, received 137 quotations for DRAM, NAND Flash and controller chips from 12 suppliers. Each supplier used different part numbers, currencies and delivery terms. His team had to open every Excel file, reconcile it against the BOM and request clarification by email. This manual, chạy bằng cơm process concealed three risks: abnormal price increases, unfavorable payment terms and excessive dependence on one supplier. When DRAM prices move weekly, a report completed two days later may already be obsolete. The ERP records transactions, but it cannot recognize that differently formatted component codes refer to the same SKU. 2.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.excerpt: "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."
articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
